title: Half of residual heat variation came from 22-39 monthly records in four Atlantic and Pacific coral samples in 2003-2019
abstract: We tested how much of a coral heat slope came from a small part of the survey record. Four Atlantic and Pacific samples from 2003-2019 had 5,336 monthly records at sites observed in two or more years. After control for site, year, month and depth, 22-39 records supplied half of squared residual heat variation in each sample. These records were 1.2-5.3 percent of each sample. The inverse sum of squared shares was 54-89 records. Removing the top five percent and fitting the model again changed slopes but left all four positive. This calculation measures design concentration. It does not show that high-share records are wrong or that they cause bias. Selected surveys, missing outcomes, few error clusters and one reporting system limit inference. The result does not measure species loss, pollution effects or a causal climate effect. Code, source hashes, survey evidence, checks and a figure are included.

display.caption: Left: the share of squared residual heat variation, ranked from largest to smallest. The plot shows the first 30 percent of records. The dotted line shows equal shares. Right: fitted heat slopes before and after removal of the top one or five percent of records. Points have no uncertainty bars; intervals are in estimates.csv. Removal changes the fitted contrast and is not a bias correction.

citations.reason: Prior severe-bleaching support audit gives the repeated-site scope. We rebuild from raw data and test design concentration for mean bleaching. Records overlap.
Prior prediction test reports limited heat support. Our test measures residual heat information in fixed-effect models, not forecast skill.
